PCN Level 2 Examination Guide & Practice Questions

Prepare for PCN Level 2 NDT certification with 25 practice questions on multiple inspection methods and defect detection techniques.

By Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III · March 21, 2026

About This Exam

PCN (Personal Certification Scheme for Non-Destructive Testing) Level 2 certification validates intermediate competence in NDT across various methods. The exam contains 75 multiple-choice questions requiring 70% pass rate (approximately 53 correct) within 2 hours. It is typically open-book, allowing reference to relevant standards and guidelines. Prerequisites include completion of Level 1 in the specific NDT method and minimum 6 months full-time experience or equivalent part-time experience.

Key Topics Covered

Method-Specific Theory and Principles

PCN Level 2 requires solid understanding of the fundamental principles underlying your chosen NDT method (UT, RT, MT, PT, ET, VT). Knowledge of equipment operation, material properties affecting inspection, and detection capabilities is essential.

Discontinuity Recognition and Interpretation

Identifying defects in realistic inspection scenarios distinguishes competent from exceptional inspectors. Understanding how different discontinuities appear in your method and recognizing false indications is critical.

Calibration and Measurement Procedures

Proper equipment calibration ensures reliable measurements. Understanding reference standards, calibration procedures, linearity checks, and sensitivity verification guides effective inspection practice.

Safety and Regulatory Compliance

Working safely while performing NDT is paramount. Knowledge of hazards specific to each method, regulatory requirements, and safety procedures protects both the inspector and others.

Reporting and Documentation

Professional documentation of findings supports quality assurance and traceability. Understanding what to record, how to measure defects, and proper reporting formats ensures complete information capture.

Standards and Acceptance Criteria

Different applications require different acceptance criteria. Understanding how criteria are selected and applied guides proper inspection and reporting decisions.

Practice Questions

1. PCN Level 2 requires minimum experience of:
A. 3 months
B. 6 months full-time (or equivalent)
C. 1 year
D. 2 years

2. The primary difference between PCN and ASNT certification is:
A. PCN is European; ASNT is North American
B. PCN requires less experience
C. ASNT is only for pressure equipment
D. They cover identical material

3. A Level 2 inspector is qualified to:
A. Operate equipment and perform inspections
B. Interpret results and produce reports
C. Develop procedures
D. A and B

4. PCN certification is valid for how long?
A. 3 years
B. 5 years
C. Permanently
D. 2 years

5. The primary benefit of international NDT certification (PCN, ASNT, ISO 9712) is:
A. Higher salary only
B. Reciprocal recognition across countries and industries
C. Exemption from company training
D. No need for continuing education

6. When performing ultrasonic thickness measurement per PCN standards:
A. Only one measurement per area is needed
B. Multiple measurements at different locations establish pattern
C. Surface finish doesn't matter
D. No calibration is required

7. A radiographic indication with sharp, well-defined edges typically represents:
A. Porosity
B. Lack of fusion
C. A tight crack
D. Corrosion

8. Magnetic particle testing cannot effectively detect:
A. Surface cracks
B. Near-surface porosity
C. Defects parallel to magnetic field
D. Fatigue cracks

9. In penetrant testing, penetrant dwell time typically ranges from:
A. 1-3 minutes
B. 5-30 minutes
C. 60-90 minutes
D. Overnight

10. Surface cleanliness in penetrant testing is:
A. Somewhat important
B. Critical to detection reliability
C. Only matters for visible dye
D. Not important if developer is applied

11. The "dead zone" in ultrasonic testing:
A. Is the area near the transducer where signals cannot be properly received
B. Represents material that cannot be inspected
C. Increases with probe frequency
D. Cannot be reduced

12. A weld defect acceptance level per ISO standards depends on:
A. Welder name
B. Application and consequence of failure
C. Shift when the weld was made
D. Cost of the product

13. When a defect approaches acceptance limit size, the appropriate action is:
A. Reject immediately
B. Accept despite uncertainty
C. Measure carefully against specification and document
D. Retest with different method

14. False indications in NDT typically result from:
A. Equipment malfunction
B. Surface conditions or material properties not related to defects
C. Operator error exclusively
D. Natural test variability

15. ISO 5817 weld defect classification system organizes defects by:
A. Size only
B. Defect type
C. Metal composition
D. Date of manufacturing

16. When reporting NDT findings, the level 2 inspector must document:
A. Equipment used
B. Date, time, location of inspection
C. Defects identified with location and size
D. All of the above

17. The purpose of reference standards in NDT is:
A. Prove the material is good quality
B. Establish measurement baselines and comparison targets
C. Determine acceptance criteria
D. Train operators

18. Probability of Detection (POD) in NDT refers to:
A. How likely equipment is to malfunction
B. Likelihood of finding a defect if one exists
C. Frequency of false indications
D. Probability the part will fail

19. When a PCN Level 2 inspector identifies a defect beyond their judgment:
A. They must make a decision anyway
B. Report findings to Level 3 or supervisor for evaluation
C. Assume the part is acceptable
D. Test again with a different method

20. Risk-based inspection prioritizes inspection resources by:
A. Equipment age
B. Consequence and probability of failure
C. Operator preference
D. Convenience

21. The "sensitivity" of an NDT method describes:
A. How easily the operator is confused
B. The smallest defect that can be reliably detected
C. Equipment cost
D. Inspection speed

22. When equipment fails calibration, the appropriate action is:
A. Continue inspections anyway
B. Stop inspections until equipment is repaired and recalibrated
C. Use it for training only
D. Document and continue with caution

23. Continuing education for PCN certification is:
A. Optional
B. Required for renewal
C. Only for Level 3
D. Not specified in PCN scheme

24. The relationship between defect size and inspectability is:
A. Smaller defects are always easier to detect
B. Size is unrelated to detection difficulty
C. Smaller defects are harder to detect; inspectability depends on defect type and NDT method
D. Only very large defects matter

25. A primary responsibility of Level 2 inspectors is to:
A. Develop new NDT procedures
B. Train operators
C. Perform reliable inspections and produce accurate reports
D. Approve all inspection programs

Answer Key with Explanations

1. Answer: B (6 months full-time)
PCN Level 2 requires minimum 6 months full-time NDT experience in the specific method, or equivalent part-time experience (typically 12 months part-time).

2. Answer: A (PCN is European; ASNT is North American)
PCN (UK/Europe) and ASNT (North America) are separate certification bodies with different schemes. ASNT is more common in the US; PCN in UK and Europe.

3. Answer: D (A and B)
Level 2 inspectors can independently perform inspections, operate equipment, interpret results, and produce professional reports without Level 3 supervision.

4. Answer: A (3 years)
PCN certification is valid 3 years. Renewal requires proof of continuing professional development (CPD) hours or retesting.

5. Answer: B (Reciprocal recognition across countries and industries)
International certifications like PCN, ASNT, and ISO 9712 allow professionals to work across different regions and industries with portable qualifications.

6. Answer: B (Multiple measurements at different locations establish pattern)
Effective thickness measurement requires multiple UT readings to determine if thinning is uniform (general corrosion) or localized (pitting). Single measurements can miss critical areas.

7. Answer: C (A tight crack)
Tight cracks produce sharp, well-defined radiographic indications because they represent clear density changes without gradient. Broader defects show diffuse patterns.

8. Answer: C (Defects parallel to magnetic field)
This is the fundamental limitation of MT. Defects parallel to field lines don't create perpendicular field distortion and therefore don't attract particles.

9. Answer: B (5-30 minutes)
Standard dwell time for PT is 5-30 minutes depending on defect size expectations. Longer dwells ensure small defects capture sufficient penetrant; shorter times suffice for larger defects.

10. Answer: B (Critical to detection reliability)
Surface cleanliness is the most critical factor in PT. Contaminants completely block penetrant entry, making the inspection completely ineffective regardless of technique quality.

11. Answer: A (Is the area near the transducer where signals cannot be properly received)
The dead zone exists because the transducer continues vibrating after transmission, preventing reception of signals from very close reflectors (like shallow surface defects).

12. Answer: B (Application and consequence of failure)
Codes recognize that critical applications require stricter acceptance than non-critical. Level A (strictest) for critical; Level C (most permissive) for non-critical per ISO standards.

13. Answer: C (Measure carefully against specification and document)
Borderline defects require careful, objective measurement and comparison against acceptance criteria. Documentation supports traceability and decision justification.

14. Answer: B (Surface conditions or material properties not related to defects)
False indications come from roughness, geometry changes, material characteristics, etc. Distinguishing real defects requires understanding what causes false indications in your method.

15. Answer: B (Defect type)
ISO 5817 organizes defects by type (cracks, porosity, inclusions, lack of fusion, etc.). Size limits and acceptance criteria then apply to each type at different levels (A, B, C).

16. Answer: D (All of the above)
Professional inspection reports include equipment identification, date/time/location of work, defects with precise location/size descriptions, and inspector identification for traceability.

17. Answer: B (Establish measurement baselines and comparison targets)
Reference standards allow comparison of unknown indications against known defect responses, guiding severity assessment and acceptance decisions.

18. Answer: B (Likelihood of finding a defect if one exists)
POD is a statistical measure of inspection system effectiveness. High POD (e.g., 90%) means the method will find 90% of relevant defects if present.

19. Answer: B (Report findings to Level 3 or supervisor for evaluation)
Level 2 professionals perform and report inspections but don't make complex judgment calls beyond their training. Unclear or borderline cases go to Level 3 for definitive decision.

20. Answer: B (Consequence and probability of failure)
RBI focuses resources on systems where failure would be most damaging (high consequence) or most likely (high probability), maximizing safety impact per dollar spent.

21. Answer: B (The smallest defect that can be reliably detected)
Method sensitivity determines the minimum defect size that produces detectable indications. Higher sensitivity detects smaller defects; lower sensitivity misses small flaws.

22. Answer: B (Stop inspections until equipment is repaired and recalibrated)
Failed calibration means measurements are unreliable. Continuing inspections produces untrustworthy data. Repairs and recalibration must precede resume operations.

23. Answer: B (Required for renewal)
PCN requires documented continuing professional development (CPD) to maintain current knowledge and skills. Renewal without CPD or retesting is not permitted.

24. Answer: C (Smaller defects are harder to detect; inspectability depends on defect type and NDT method)
Small defects produce smaller indications in most NDT methods, making them harder to distinguish from noise. Detection difficulty also depends on defect orientation, location, and method sensitivity.

25. Answer: C (Perform reliable inspections and produce accurate reports)
Level 2 is the competent practitioner level. The primary responsibility is producing accurate, professionally documented inspection results that support quality assurance.

Study Tips & Exam Strategy

1. Review PCN Scheme Requirements: Understand PCN structure, Level 1/2/3 differences, certification validity, and continuing education requirements.

2. Master Your Method: Deep knowledge of your chosen NDT method (UT, MT, PT, RT, ET, or VT) is essential. Study specific method theory, equipment, and application.

3. Study Defect Recognition: Become proficient identifying defect types in your method. Study actual inspection data, photographs, and radiographs.

4. Learn International Standards: ISO standards (5817, 9712, 11699) are referenced throughout PCN. Understand classification systems and acceptance criteria.

5. Understand Risk and Reliability: PCN emphasizes POD, RBI, and probability concepts. Understand how inspection system effectiveness is evaluated.

6. Practice Report Writing: Level 2 must produce professional reports. Practice clear, complete documentation that captures all relevant information.

7. Complete Practice Exams: Take full-length exams under timed conditions to assess readiness and identify weak knowledge areas.

Recommended Study Resources

Required Documents: PCN Scheme Rules, ISO 5817, ISO 9712, relevant method-specific standards (ASTM or BS)

Key References: ASNT Nondestructive Testing Handbook (relevant volume), NDT method manufacturer training materials, ISO standard specifications

Training: PCN approved Level 2 courses for your specific method, manufacturer-provided equipment training, supervised field experience

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Can I pursue PCN if I'm already ASNT certified?
A: Yes, certifications are complementary. Some professionals hold both ASNT and PCN certifications. Experience in one can support obtaining the other.

Q: How much continuing education is required?
A: PCN typically requires 18-24 hours CPD per 3-year cycle. This ensures professionals stay current with evolving techniques and standards.

Q: Is PCN recognized in North America?
A: PCN is less common in the US but growing in recognition. ASNT remains dominant in North America, while PCN is standard in UK and Europe.

Q: What's the pass rate for Level 2?
A: With proper preparation and relevant experience, 75-85% pass on first attempt. PCN is considered comparable in difficulty to ASNT Level II.

Q: Can I get PCN Level 3 without Level 2?
A: Generally no. PCN structure requires sequential progression from Level 1 to 2 to 3. Equivalent experience may allow some substitution but typically Level 2 is prerequisite.
